#7843. Arkansas S. Ct.: Legislature May Revive Cases Barred by Statute of Limitations

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The court reverses its precedent, dating back to 1846, that held such revival unconstitutionally restricted the defendant's "vested rights" not to be sued, which had been created by the earlier statute of limitations.

From H.C. v. Nesmith, decided last week by the Arkansas Supreme Court, in an opinion by Justice Nicholas Bronni, joined by Justices Courtney Rae Hudson, Cody Hiland, and Rhonda Wood (note that other state courts are split on this question, see, e.g., this post and this one):

This case presents a particularly important question: Can the General Assembly extend the statute of limitations in cases where it has already run and afford child-sex-abuse victims an opportunity to hold their abusers accountable? … [T]his court's vested-rights precedent … categorically bars "expand[ing] a limitation period so as to revive a claim already barred." …

Revisiting our vested-rights precedent, we conclude that it lacks any constitutional basis and, as such, cannot stand. We therefore overrule our prior cases prohibiting the legislature from expanding a limitations period and thereby reviving time-barred claims [and] uphold the Vulnerable Victims of Sex Abuse Act against Nesmith's constitutional challenge ….

[Under] our vested-rights precedent …, "the legislature cannot expand a statute of limitation so as to revive a cause of action already barred." That doctrine rests on the assumption that when a civil statute of limitations runs, a tortfeasor has a vested right to the property that could have been the subject of a potential claim….

[But] our cases do not cite any constitutional basis for that doctrine. Far from it, when we first employed that principle to strike down legislation in 1933, we instead relied on a single legal encyclopedia published in 1915 assuring us that—at that sole moment in time—most jurisdictions held that legislatures could not revive a claim after a statute-of-limitations defense had run. Or, perhaps more generously, we relied on that legal encyclopedia plus an unreasoned extension of this court's prior case law suggesting that to retroactively alter an applicable statute of limitations, the legislature needed to speak clearly and show it had considered the consequences. That approach, unbound by actual text or constitutional history, is not consistent with our constitutional role….

To be sure, some later cases—perhaps recognizing that our earlier cases do not cite any constitutional language supporting our vested-rights precedent—suggest that precedent rests on due-process principles…. [But] that label does not work because the expiration of a statute-of-limitations period does not confer a property right—or any other right for that matter.

As the Supreme Court has explained in rejecting similar arguments under the federal due process clause, a statute-of-limitations period merely governs the time within which a claim must be brought, see Chase Sec. Corp. v. Donaldson (1945); it does not reflect a legislative judgment "that [a] defendant should 'be free from liability after the legislatively determined period of time.'" Instead, these limitations "are by definition arbitrary" and rest entirely on legislative judgments about how best to encourage plaintiffs to diligently pursue claims and avoid litigation "after memories have faded, witnesses have died or disappeared, and evidence has been lost."

As such, they "represent a public policy [choice] about" how to balance those interests and exist only by "legislative grace." Altering that period and establishing a different, equally "arbitrary" date does not—contrary to our prior case law's unfounded assertion—deprive a defendant of any vested property right. Rather, balancing competing interests and "resolv[ing] the debate" about when a claim should be time-barred is precisely the kind of thing that our constitution leaves "to the legislature."

We therefore hold that the court's vested-rights precedent has no basis in law, and we overrule our prior cases categorically barring the legislature from expanding the limitations period and thereby reviving claims. Indeed, as we recently reaffirmed, "we are bound by constitutional text," not precedent that "treats our constitution not as a written document but as a set of civic values and norms determined by judges." And we now restore to the General Assembly its constitutional power to decide how long is too long to bring a claim….

Recognizing the vital importance of stare decisis, I nonetheless conclude that this is an exceptional case that warrants breaking with our precedent. Before the General Assembly enacted the Justice for Vulnerable Victims of Sexual Abuse Act, victims of sexual abuse who were under age twenty-one generally had until three years after attaining full age to file suit. Yet childhood sexual abuse presents a unique problem in that—by its very nature—it often prevents victims from bringing timely claims. This consideration leads me to conclude that great injury and injustice will result if we continue to follow our vested-rights precedent in this case….

In recent years, research has revealed the prevalence of childhood sexual abuse and some of the reasons for delayed reporting. For example, we now know that at least one in four girls and one in twenty boys in the United States experience child sexual abuse. Even still, childhood sexual abuse is vastly underreported, and when it is reported, often years or decades have passed. Victims may be reluctant to come forward due to the negative repercussions of disclosure, such as disruptions in family stability, loss of close relationships, or involvement with the authorities; fear of not being believed; and psychological obstacles such as shame and self-blame….

I disagree with the majority's decision to upend 180 years of this court's precedent prohibiting legislative attempts to revive expired statutes of limitation…. In my view, applying our vested-rights precedent to the present case, … the legislature lacked the power to revive the expired statute of limitations applicable to Nesmith, and therefore, the claims against Nesmith were time-barred.

[I]n 1846 this court in Couch v. McKee treated the completed bar [of the statute of limitations] as a property interest that cannot be removed by later legislation. When the statute has run, the defendant's right to be free from the claim becomes part of his or her protected legal estate, an interest the State cannot simply reassign by retroactive enactment. Our later cases have repeatedly applied that same rule, holding that revival statutes cannot constitutionally divest a defendant of a vested limitations defense.

Nor, contrary to the majority's assertion, is our vested-rights jurisprudence untethered from constitutional text. The Arkansas Constitution reflects a longstanding hostility toward retroactive laws impairing settled rights. See Ark. Const. art. 2, § 17 (prohibiting ex post facto laws and laws impairing contractual obligations); id. § 21 (protecting due process). Consistent with those principles, this court has repeatedly recognized that retroactive legislation may not constitutionally disturb vested substantive rights….

That rule is not a mere formalism. Statutes of limitation serve an important public function. They encourage the prompt filing of claims so that the truth-finding process is not impaired by faded memories, lost documents, unavailable records, and deceased witnesses. Those concerns are not hypothetical. The amicus brief filed in this case illustrates the serious prejudice that can result when claims are revived decades after the fact.

Ms. Shirley Suhl, an eighty-seven-year-old retired widow, represents that she is defending claims in federal court arising from alleged events at a facility that ceased operating around 2006 and from conduct dating back nearly forty years. She is not alleged to have personally committed sexual abuse; rather, she is alleged to have known of or been complicit in abuse by others. According to her brief, relevant facility records no longer exist, potential witnesses are elderly or deceased, and one named former employee accused of abuse is now in his nineties. Whether those allegations ultimately have merit is not before us. The point is more basic: the passage of decades can make a fair defense difficult, sometimes impossible.

This is precisely why Arkansas law has treated an accrued limitations defense as vested. Once the limitations period has run, the defendant is entitled to repose, not because the underlying allegations are unimportant but because the law recognizes that, at some point, the defense of stale claims becomes too impaired to permit reliable adjudication. The majority treats the limitations bar as a revocable act of legislative grace. Our cases have treated it differently. They have recognized that once the bar attaches, it becomes a substantive right to resist enforcement of the claim. That rule does not deny the gravity of child sexual abuse. It enforces the constitutional limit on retroactive legislation that destroys vested rights.

In this instance, stare decisis carries particular force. The rule the majority abandons today is not isolated or recently decided precedent. It can be traced back to this court's earliest jurisprudence and has been reaffirmed across generations of cases. Litigants, lawyers, and the General Assembly have long operated against that settled backdrop. Yet today, the majority discards nearly two centuries of precedent. Stability in the law matters, especially when the court alters longstanding rules governing substantive rights and retroactive legislation….

{While many judges and justices pledge full allegiance to the doctrine of stare decisis, even to the point of perpetuating clear errors of constitutional interpretation, I am not one of them. And while it is an important piece of our judicial system, I have frequently noted that "[t]his court "should not invoke stare decisis to uphold precedents that are demonstrably erroneous." Here, however, our two centuries of case law on the subject are rooted in the Arkansas Constitution as article 2 section 21 supports our precedent. Accordingly, I would follow it.

Joshua D. Gillispie (Gillispie Law Firm) and Brian G. Brooks represent plaintiffs.

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. #7835. The Best Hydroponic Systems of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

By Jenn Ryan, Katie Barton, Additional research provided by Glenda Taylor

Published Nov 11, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Hydroponic systems, which allow plants to grow in water rather than soil, are popular because they offer a way to produce a bounty of plants in a relatively small area in an indoor garden. These systems also tend to be user-friendly, so even newbie growers are likely to succeed. We recently tested eight popular models, spending several months setting them up and evaluating their various features while growing a range of plants.

We also evaluated each tested hydroponics system for its ease of use, value, functionality, appearance, and build quality. With these factors in mind, our favorite is Ahopegarden’s 10-Pod Aeroponics Growing Kit. It offers the flexibility to grow almost any type of plant, is easy to set up, and provides a good value for the money.

But Ahopegarden isn’t the only show in town. Some of the other kits we tested also ranked highly and may better fit your indoor gardening needs depending on the available space and desired setup. Check out our top picks of some of the best hydroponic systems to get started.

Bottom line: Explore the best hydroponic systems of 2026, from compact kits to large setups, each offering unique features for indoor gardening success.

To qualify as one of our top picks, we required each hydroponic system to have a water circulation system to keep the water fresh. When evaluating all-inclusive systems, we looked for bright grow lights that could be adjusted in height as the plants grow taller. The following hydroponic systems vary in design and size, but each is well suited to growing healthy herbs and plants indoors.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Appearance 4/5; Functionality 5/5; Build Quality 4/5; Value 5/5

The Ahopegarden offers an affordable way to grow fruits, vegetables, or flowers at home. It has the capacity to grow 10 plants and comes with baskets, sponges, plant food, and grow domes—everything needed to get started except for seeds. While this system can be used to produce any type of plant, the adjustable light reaches a maximum height of 14.6 inches, so users will need to select plant varieties that won’t exceed this.

We chose a dwarf tomato variety and mini bell pepper to grow in our Ahopegarden, planting five of each seed. Setting the system up required us to soak the sponges, fill the water tank, and use tweezers to add 2 to 3 seeds to each sponge (some larger seeds must be soaked for 6 to 12 hours before planting). We added grow domes to our plant pods and selected the “vegetable” button on the top of the light panel, which put the grow light on the appropriate timer.

We love this system’s flexibility. It’s also on the smaller side, so it’s easy to find a spot for it, even in cramped spaces. Our biggest concern is that there isn’t much spacing between the pods, so depending on the plant, it can get crowded.

What our tester says: “The Ahopegarden was simple to set up. We love that it has automatic lights for growing fruits and flowers or vegetables. We planted dwarf tomatoes and mini bell peppers in our growing kit, and they sprouted within a week.”—Katie Barton, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Ahopegarden hydroponic system at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Setup 4/5; Appearance 4/5; Functionality 4/5; Build Quality 4/5; Value 4/5

The AeroGarden Bounty grows up to nine plants and comes with a seed kit of the user’s choice. Thanks to a convenient touch screen, growers can easily set their own light and watering schedule, and there’s a vacation mode for when the system will be unattended.

One of the system’s best features is its tall grow height of 24 inches—the highest of any smaller hydroponic system in our lineup. The grow height makes it easier to nurture larger plant varieties, such as peppers and tomatoes, without worrying about plants getting their leaves singed on the lights. The system also includes a trellis, which is helpful when growing such larger plants.

The Bounty has a large water reservoir, so the system needs minimal topping off. It also comes with liquid plant food and humidity caps for seeds to germinate. However, in testing—growing a combination of lettuces and herbs—the width of the system proved a bit short. This led to stunted growth of some plants, while others competed for light. For example, when we placed cilantro and a short lettuce variety next to each other, the cilantro grew taller and blocked light from the lettuce, which failed to truly thrive.

While AeroGarden could fix this problem by making the Bounty wider, we found the solution to be simply using fewer grow stations simultaneously. When replanting seeds in the system during a second round of testing, we planted fewer plants (six instead of nine) and found that they did better, growing larger and looking healthier.

What our tester says: “Despite the width of the system being a bit short for my preferences, after I figured out how to work around this issue, the AeroGarden Bounty earned one of the best overall spots for the number of plants it grows, its reasonable price, its tall grow height, and for being an inclusive kit that makes hydroponics simple.”—Jenn Ryan, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the AeroGarden Bounty hydroponic system at Amazon or AeroGarden.

Our Ratings: Setup 4/5; Appearance 5/5; Functionality 5/5; Build Quality 4/5; Value 5/5

Few gardening processes are more straightforward than taking cuttings from existing houseplants or vines and starting them in water. The TomGear hydroponic garden includes three see-through glass bulbs to fill with water to encourage root development. Its wood framing also serves as an attractive decoration for a sunny windowsill or countertop.

While the system doesn’t include LED lights or a water-recirculating pump, it works via a tried-and-true plant-propagation method that is simple but effective. When roots develop, plants can be transplanted into pots or to an outdoor garden spot.

During testing, we found this system was very easy to set up. We also appreciated its small size and good looks; it could beautify just about any spot that gets enough natural light for plants. However, we found the necks of the glass vases to be quite narrow—while we could easily fit herbs (such as the rosemary we rooted), we had trouble getting snake plants and succulents into the water. That issue aside, this system gets high marks for its affordability, attractiveness, simple setup, and effectiveness in helping plants grow roots.

Get the TomGear hydroponic garden at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Appearance 4/5; Functionality 5/5; Build Quality 5/5; Value 5/5

The Lettuce Grow Farmstand has the capacity for 36 full-size plants, making it the largest hydroponic system on our list. It comes with a teardrop-shaped base that can hold 20 gallons of water, which means we didn’t have to top off the water reservoir as often as with some of the smaller systems.

This hydroponic tower system is adjustable—gardeners can add or remove sections as desired to increase or decrease the number of plants from as few as 18 and as many as 36 plants. Despite its impressive size, the Farmstand proved to have a simple assembly process. It uses a single durable plastic pipe that runs through the center of the system. It comes with two timers, one for lights and one for the water pump, which can be set and then left alone, making it simple to set up.

This vertical hydroponic garden is not restricted to indoor use; growers can choose whether or not to purchase lights (which are not necessary when the system is used outdoors). Plant food, a pH kit, and a pH-down solution (to test and adjust the system’s pH) are included, but Lettuce Grow systems do not come with seeds or plants. Gardeners do have the option to purchase seedlings (sprouted plants ready to put into the system) from the company. While the seedlings were expensive, they were in perfect condition when they arrived, and we did not have a single plant die throughout the testing process.

Get the Lettuce Grow hydroponic system at Amazon or Lettuce Grow.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Appearance 5/5; Functionality 4.5/5; Build Quality 4/5; Value 4/5

The Click & Grow is an attractive indoor garden ideal for beginners or those with limited space. It comes with everything a user needs to get started, including plant pods, grow domes, and easy-to-follow instructions.

This small hydroponic system was a breeze to set up. All we had to do was insert the plant packs into the pods, add water, and plug the unit in. It automatically cycles the light 16 hours on and 8 hours off and utilizes a water level float to notify users when to add more water. Since the nutrients are included in the plant pods, there’s no need to add special fertilizer to the tank. The basil pods included in our hydroponic herb garden kit sprouted within a few days and have continued to grow large and healthily. The only maintenance we’ve had to perform is adding water to the tank about every two weeks.

Click & Grow offers more than 75 plant varieties and also sells seedless pods for growers who prefer to use their own seeds. We appreciate that the two included extension arms allow for plants up to 18.5 inches tall. This hydroponics grow kit was one of our favorite, easy-to-use indoor gardens. Our only complaint is that it’s a little pricey considering there is only room for three plant pods.

Get the Click & Grow hydroponics system at Amazon.

Our Ratings: Setup 5/5; Appearance 4/5; Functionality 4.5/5; Build Quality 3/5; Value 3.5/5

Even newbies can stretch their green thumb with this system from leading hydroponic systems manufacturer AeroGarden. The Harvest 2.0 indoor herb garden provides everything necessary to care for its six growing stations. We loved the simple setup: Gardeners simply insert plant pods, add water and plant food, plug in the unit, and it’s ready to grow. Humidity caps to help germinate seeds when starting the system are included.

This hydroponics growing system comes with six plastic pots and six seed plugs that are preseeded (Italian basil, Thai basil, parsley, dill, thyme, and mint) and ready to go. Liquid plant nutrients are also included. For convenience, the Harvest automates both lighting and water circulation. The system turns the LED grow lights on for 15 hours per day, though users can turn the lights on and off manually as well. Water circulation is automatic, and the unit features both a low-water and a time-to-add-nutrients indicator to take the guesswork out of indoor hydroponics.

One downside to this indoor hydroponic garden is that it lacks an adjustable light timer—the lights simply come on for 15 hours a day, then turn off until the cycle starts again. The height of the light hood is limited, too. It only offers about 12 inches for plants to grow, which may prove too short for the herbs. Our dill and our basil, for instance, were damaged because they grew too tall and pressed against the hot light before we could harvest them.

Get the AeroGarden Harvest hydroponic system at Amazon.

Plantaform’s Smart Indoor Garden is a fogponics system that turns a fertilizer and water mixture into fog, delivering nutrients to the plant’s root system. It comes with 15 pods, a lettuce mix plant pack, germination domes, and plant food. Six other plant pack varieties are available for purchase separately.

When we received the Plantaform grow kit, we were impressed by its quality, futuristic look. While it’s a bit larger, at about two feet tall and almost two feet in diameter, we positioned it in the middle of our dining room table. The instructions for setting it up weren’t quite as clear as those for other growing systems we tried. However, once we figured out what to do, it only took about fifteen minutes to get everything set up.

Our lettuce seeds sprouted within a few days, and we were able to remove the germination domes. We then relied on the app to inform us when to add water and nutrients and harvest the plants. Unfortunately, the app malfunctioned a few times, telling us to harvest at one week and then again at two weeks when the plants were still tiny. We decided to ignore these notifications and wait until the plants were at least 40 to 45 days, as suggested on the Plantaform website. Despite issues with the app, keeping up with this hydroponic setup was as easy as refilling the water tank every two and a half weeks, and our lettuce plants grew to be lush and healthy.

Get the Plantaform hydroponics system at Plantaform.

When evaluating these hydroponic home garden systems, we considered over a dozen companies and looked at the brand, customer reviews, features of the product, extra items included, and how well the system grew plants. We also looked at durability and ease of use when testing and evaluating these products.

We scored each product using a rubric that evaluated the watering system, how well the plants in the system thrived, how easy the system was to set up and use, any extra features the product included, types of plants the system could grow, the durability of the product, and how attractive the setup was. We also considered the cost value of each product.

As we tested each hydroponic system, we looked closely at how well the plants grew and how easy the system was to use and maintain. To do this, we tested each system for a minimum of a month, and some of the systems were tested for over a year.

Plants need four essential elements to thrive: water, oxygen, light, and nutrients. A successful hydroponic system must supply an adequate amount of all four. For those new to cultivating an indoor garden, the options may seem confusing, but today’s manufacturers offer various types of hydroponic systems that automate much of the process.

While all hydroponic systems supply plant roots with water and nutrients, the method varies. There are six common types of hydroponic systems, all with unique strong points, but some are better suited to commercial settings than DIY home settings.

Hydroponic gardening at home is not difficult, but the operator will need basic knowledge about how hydroponics work. This means, for most systems, that growers should have some experience in sprouting plants from seeds, knowing when plants need plant food, monitoring the water flow of the reservoir, and adjusting nutrient levels and pH.

Fortunately, with today’s consumer hydroponic systems, indoor gardening is simple and straightforward. Systems like the popular AeroGarden come with mesh pods and soilless medium (often coconut coir plugs), as well as a pump for circulating water and keeping roots moist and healthy. Unlike classic terrariums, most of today’s in-home systems also feature grow lights on timers that provide the correct amount of light for optimal growth.

One of the convenient characteristics of a hydroponic grow system is that users can grow more plants in less space because the roots don’t need to spread out to seek nutrients. Depending on the type of setup, hydroponic systems can be as small as a few inches deep by a few inches wide or as big as a few feet deep by a few feet wide. The most common models, such as the AeroGarden Harvest, can fit on a kitchen countertop, ladder plant stand, or a table and take up no more than 1 to 2 square feet of space—yet some models can grow up to 30 full-size plants.

Indoor hydroponic systems can grow a wide variety of plant types. While smaller systems, such as the AeroGarden, are best used for herbs and smaller varieties of peppers and tomatoes, larger systems like the Lettuce Grow Farmstand can grow virtually anything, including large lettuces, full-size tomato or pepper plants, kale, Swiss chard, bok choy, and even cabbage. Flowers can be grown in hydroponic systems, too.

Consistent temperature is essential to plant growth, so commercial hydroponic growers often have water heaters to regulate the water temperature. However, in-home hydroponic systems don’t require the same temperature-control level because they’re usually placed in a home where the temperature remains between 60 and 80 degrees Fahrenheit. Many experts suggest that the optimal water temperature for plant growth is between 68 and 71.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

Unlike self-watering planter systems, a soilless growing medium is normally used in hydroponic gardening. These mediums can include coconut coir plugs or mineral wool. However, some systems, such as the Lettuce Grow Farmstand, have plants that are started in actual soil and then transplanted into small pods to grow without additional soil in the hydroponic system.

Some systems come with plants or seeds already in the substrate. As the plants grow, the roots extend below the pod into the reservoir or channel beneath.

Nutrients used in hydroponic systems can be in either powder or liquid form. Some come with powders that must be dissolved in warm water before being added to the water reservoir, while other systems come with liquid plant food that can be poured directly into the reservoir.

Automated hydroponic systems require minimal maintenance relative to a traditional garden or a DIY hydroponics system. Most systems recommend topping off the tank reservoir about once a week and adding plant food at the same time. It’s also recommended that the reservoir be cleaned every month or so to prevent the buildup of algae in the tank.

During the growing cycle, users may also need to wipe down the unit’s surface with a clean, damp rag to maintain its appearance—they aren’t immune to dust!

There are many advantages to owning a hydroponic grow kit, including water conservation, reduced risk of pest problems, and fresh produce year-round.

According to Dr. Michael B. Timmons, professor emeritus and graduate professor in the Department of Biological and Environmental Engineering at Cornell University, “Producing food as efficiently as possible and minimizing the use of our scarce resources should be a goal for everyone. Each family could contribute toward this goal by choosing to produce some or all of the vegetables they eat. Producing vegetables hydroponically using controlled environment agriculture (CEA) … uses 90 percent less water and land than conventional agriculture.” He goes on to say that those who grow some of their food hydroponically can reduce the associated carbon footprint by producing in their own home, garage, or mini-greenhouse.

As explained by the Oklahoma State University Extension, one of the advantages of utilizing a hydroponic system to grow vegetables and flowers is being able to control the nutrients and growing environment. Hydroponic systems also reduce the risk of chemical exposure due to pesticides as well as the risk of pests infesting the plants and soil (although the plants are not immune to pests that may travel indoors). Finally, with an all-inclusive hydroponic system, growing herbs, fruits, veggies, or flowers indoors needn’t take a lot of time or require a large garden or a sunny window.

Because hydroponic systems automate the growing process, users don’t need a lot of gardening or hydroponic knowledge to enjoy fresh herbs and produce. For those new to growing indoors, however, some questions are to be expected. Read on for answers that provide basic info.

For those just developing a green thumb, an affordable hydroponics system that automates lighting and watering and provides a few growing stations is ideal.

Most systems come with built-in aeration via a pump, so additional aeration is not needed.

No. Nutrient solutions are preformulated to offer the best pH level for a wide variety of plants and herbs. However, you may want to test the pH level of the water in the reservoir with a pH test kit and add pH-adjusting liquid to raise or lower the pH level to about 6 or 7, which is the ideal range for growing vegetables and herbs.

To maintain a strict pH level, pH-adjusting liquids are available, and a couple of drops of either “pH Up” or “pH Down” can change the level. Some hydroponic systems come with a testing kit, but these are often a separate purchase.

Yes. Each indoor growing system has its own recommendations on how often to clean it, and some systems recommend cleaning as often as once a month. In general, cleaning requires removing all the spent plants and scrubbing or wiping out the unit—especially the water reservoir—before using it again. Apart from that, wipe down the surfaces with a clean, damp rag as necessary to remove dust, plant debris, and grime.

#7833. The Best Lunch Boxes for Construction Workers, Picks from Our Editors

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 11, 2026 9:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Lunch boxes for construction workers need to keep food fresh, but they must also be highly portable and durable to meet the demands of their environments. Fortunately, there are hundreds of models on the market to choose from, whether you’re looking for an insulated option for a cold sandwich and salad or an electric lunch box to keep your food hot.

To help you choose the right construction lunch box from the many options available, we researched the pros and cons of various lunch box materials and designs and reached out to two experts for their opinions. Based on our research and their insights, we chose the Arctic Zone Titan 16 Can Zipperless Hardbody Cooler as our top choice for its tough construction, easy-to-clean interior, and convenient shoulder strap. Below, you’ll find our reviews on the rest of our top picks of the best lunch boxes for construction workers and details on which features matter most when selecting the right one.

Bottom line: Find the perfect lunch box for construction workers with our top picks, balancing durability, portability, and functionality.

The following lunch boxes for work have been assigned different awards to make it easier to focus on specific feature sets. We’ve included everything from heated lunch boxes to those that have a separate compartment or multiple compartments to keep hot meals organized away from water bottles. If you’re looking for gifts for construction workers or a professional lunch box for yourself, our top picks have got you covered.

Choosing the single best lunch box for construction workers was challenging, but the Arctic Zone cooler boasts several user-friendly features, offers good durability, and is also affordable.

At first glance, it looks like a soft-sided cooler, but the exterior fabric contains a solid, leakproof liner that actually makes it a hard-sided model. Its main compartment has a removable SmartShelf you can use to divide the interior space so hard items like water bottles don’t crush soft things like sandwiches The zipper-free lid flips over to provide fast and easy access to the cooler’s contents. There is also an insulated front pocket and a mesh pocket on each end.

The Arctic Zone cooler has a thick base designed to keep ice for up to 2 days. Though the 16-can version has quite a large capacity, it’s actually quite comfortable to carry thanks to its padded, adjustable shoulder strap.

Get the Arctic Zone lunch box for construction workers (various colors and sizes) at Amazon, Target, or Arctic Zone.

Few materials are tougher than steel, and since production costs are relatively low, this Stanley classic lunch box is both rugged and budget-conscious. Though a basic model, it boasts a durable construction and a clip in the lid that can hold Stanley’s classic insulated vacuum bottle or other similar-sized containers. It has two metal latches that provide firm, secure closure and a sturdy handle that makes it easy to carry.

With a 10-quart capacity, there’s ample room for food, but this no-frills hard shell lunch box lacks insulation. So consider this sturdy, well-priced model a solid choice for traditional lunches of sandwiches, subs, and snacks. This model also comes in a few color options to suit individual user preferences.

Get the Stanley Classic lunch box for construction workers (various colors) at Amazon.

Milwaukee is known for its pro-grade jobsite tools, so who better to create a women’s and men’s work lunch box that’s durable enough for heavy-duty conditions? There’s plenty of space inside the high-capacity, soft-sided cooler to hold and food and beverages for a hard day’s work. The dual-layer insulation can keep ice for up to 24 hours, and there are five separate compartments in the lid and sides for dry food and snacks.

The exterior is made of tear-resistant 1680D ballistic material, and this builders’ lunch bag also has a hard, impact-resistant base. All hardware is metal rather than plastic to enable long-term use, and it has a tape measure clip that doubles as a bottle opener as well as a padded shoulder strap.

Get the Milwaukee lunch box for construction workers at Amazon, Ace Hardware, The Home Depot, or Northern Tool + Equipment.

Klein is respected in the construction and contractor trades for producing high-quality hand and power tools, and the brand’s tough Tradesman Pro heavy-duty lunch box maintains that reputation. It features efficient insulation that can keep the contents cool (or warm) for up to 30 hours, and the hard lunch box has a weight rating of up to 300 pounds, which means it can also be used as a seat. Additionally, it has corrosion-proof stainless steel lid hinges that stay open at either 90 or 180 degrees for convenient access as you eat. One side of the lid is recessed to allow 1-liter bottles to stand upright, while the other has a useful compartment for small items like utensils and medications.

There’s a lot we love about the Klein Tools Tradesman Pro cooler, but it does have one design flaw: The strap doubles as the lid closure, but it doesn’t tighten as firmly as it could. While Klein recommends using a padlock to secure the lock hasp, that’s likely unnecessary for most jobsites. However, with its large capacity and long cooling time, this is a great lunch box for guys and gals working long shifts.

Get the Klein Tools lunch box for construction workers at Amazon, Lowe’s, The Home Depot, or Northern Tool + Equipment.

Because it’s such an effective thermal box for lunch or even a couple of day’s worth of meals, the appropriately named Igloo takes our award for the best lunch cooler. It is built to withstand the rigors of the construction site and has enough capacity for a whole crew (or your family on the weekend). It has extra-thick, efficient insulation in its body and lid and rubber latches that keep its top tightly closed.

The hard-wearing case features rustproof stainless-steel reinforcements on the handles with rubber grips for comfort. It has a stainless steel kick plate on the front for impact protection as well as oversized skid plates and tie-down points at each corner for secure transportation. Since it does have a 25-quart capacity, however, it may be best used for more than one person or a full day of meals.

Get the Igloo lunch box for construction workers (various colors) at Amazon.

Salads and sandwiches are fine during the summer, but many of us prefer hot meals when the weather starts to get cold. The Travelisimo electric lunch box is the ideal solution for the construction site. It comes with a standard 110V plug suitable for an electrical outlet or a generator. There’s also a 12V/24V vehicle cable that allows users to enjoy a warm meal on the road.

Depending on the power source and the box’s contents, thorough warming takes just 20 to 30 minutes. The outer case prevents you from burning your fingers, and the inner stainless steel container is lightweight and dishwasher safe. This heated lunch box also comes with a carry bag, a fruit box that fits inside, and a stainless steel knife and fork.

Get the Travelisimo lunch box for construction workers at Amazon.

When storage space is at a premium—at home, in the vehicle, or on the job—the CleverMade cooler offers an efficient solution. Its 24-can capacity holds a mighty big meal, and the solid base and wire support frame give reasonable structure when in use. It collapses to just 2.75 inches thick, and its patented SnapHinge makes it simple to switch between open and closed.

As a soft-sided cooler, the CleverMade doesn’t have the strength or durability of a hard-sided model, though the lined polyester fabric is lightweight and easy to wipe clean. The lunch box has handles and a strap for convenience, an incorporated bottle opener, and a large mesh pocket. Though the liner is leakproof, the insulated walls of the cooler aren’t super thick, so using blocks of ice might be smart since cubed ice won’t stay frozen long.

Get the CleverMade lunch box for construction workers at Amazon or CleverMade.

Well known for high-quality protective clothing for construction workers, Carhartt has designed its insulated lunch cooler to the same standards. The abrasion-resistant 600 denier polyester is triple stitched and protected by the brand’s Rain Defender water-repellent coating. Its zippers are the same heavyweight YKK versions used on other Carhartt products, including the best construction work pants.

The two main compartments inside this Carhartt deluxe lunch cooler provide versatile food storage and keep contents cool for 8 hours or more. You can access the top section separately from the bottom, and it also has a handy zippered pocket on the front. The bag’s handle and shoulder strap make it easy to carry, though we’re surprised the latter isn’t adjustable. Though obviously not as strong as a hard-sided model, the Carhartt cooler, one of our top lunch coolers for construction workers, is light, surprisingly rugged, and a great value.

Get the Carhartt lunch box for construction workers at Amazon.

Those who geek out on refrigerator organization will be happy to know there’s now a jobsite lunch box perfectly adapted to their preferences. The kit comes with six separate food containers (two 1.5-cup and four 2.5-cup containers), a 23-ounce shaker cup with a whisk, screw-on storage pots for supplements or protein powders, and a 7-day pill dispenser. The bag itself has a mesh pocket inside the front flap, a pocket outside, and an end pocket for the shaker cup as well as a top handle and an adjustable shoulder strap for convenient carrying. Two cooling blocks complete the comprehensive package.

Getting everything inside is a tight squeeze, and we are a little concerned about the long-term durability of the bag in tough environments. But if you like to keep all your items separate and organized and don’t mind that some of the containers are on the small side, the ThinkFit meal prep lunch bag set will be hard to beat.

Get the ThinkFit lunch box for construction workers at Amazon.

Good lunch boxes for construction workers come in all shapes and sizes, and the Tourit soft backpack cooler is a larger option that’s easy to strap to your back so your hands are free for other tools and supplies. It’s made from durable, vented waterproof fabric and has a padded back as well as padded shoulder straps. The interior features an insulated high-density foam paired with a leak-resistant liner.

Pack hot or cold food inside, and the insulation will hold the food’s temperature for up to 16 hours. Rather than using cubed ice, however, the manufacturer recommends using reusable ice packs to ensure liquids don’t leak from the zipper. In addition to its 30-can main compartment, this backpack cooler has multiple top, front, and side pockets to store not only food and drink but necessary items like your phone, keys, and wallet.

Get the Tourit lunch box for construction workers at Amazon.

To choose the right lineup of lunch boxes for the varying needs of construction workers, we considered the amount of food and drink each option could carry as well as the holding temperatures they could maintain to keep consumable items safe and fresh. Durability and portability were also top priorities, as these lunch bags and boxes must be convenient to carry yet strong enough to hold up to rugged jobsites. Though we were also careful about selecting options to fit a range of budgets, we ruled out cheaply made, low-quality lunch boxes in favor of products that offer lasting value for long-term use.

Shawna Guevara, managing director at Landmark Structural Builders, confirms much of our own thinking. “A proper lunch box for construction workers should prioritize functionality and durability,” she says. “Workers don’t need zippers that break easily, lunch boxes that retain food odors, or ones that are difficult to clean.”

As you decide which lunch box is right for you, consider these expert insights from contractor Jay Sanders of remodeling specialists Maryland Contractors regarding which features to look for when shopping for women’s and men’s lunch boxes for work. For Jay, “a tight-fitting lid that keeps food at the desired temperature for hours” and “chemical-free lunch boxes for meals that don’t harm your health” are the most important considerations.

Since lunch boxes designed for the office or coolers for the beach may not stand up to the rigors of the jobsite, evaluating construction worker lunch boxes based on the following key elements will ensure you get the right product for your needs.

Lunch boxes aren’t always treated with the greatest care. Those that have a tough outer shell will be more resistant to damage from the knocks and bumps that are part of life on a busy construction site. Hard-sided lunch boxes can help prevent food from getting smashed, and some are even strong enough to sit on while you eat. Though they are more durable, their construction can make them a bit heavier, bulkier, and less portable.

On the other hand, soft-sided and collapsible coolers are quite portable. They’re almost always lighter than hard models, are a snap to store, and are frequently less expensive. Though soft-sided coolers don’t provide as much protection for their contents as hard options, a soft lunch box can be a perfectly viable option if your lunch will wait in a vehicle rather than be toted directly to the site.

Capacity requirements largely depend on how big a meal you typically pack. A larger capacity may be more versatile—it can be used for a family weekend outing, for example. Conversely, the best small coolers will be sized just right for single-meal use as well as more portable and easier to store.

Capacity descriptions vary. Often, they are given as a number of standard beverage cans, making capacity fairly easy to visualize. Quart capacity is another common measurement. Those given in inches can make it difficult to picture the true size, so it may be smart to fold some cardboard into roughly the measurements given to avoid ordering a lunch box that’s too small or large.

Multiple compartments (as often found in bento boxes) are convenient for those who take various items for lunch and wish to keep them separated. One of our top picks even includes a pill organizer.

A well-insulated construction lunch box can keep food cool or warm for some time. However, while some manufacturers indicate how long they expect the contents to maintain temperature, their estimates may be optimistic, and there isn’t any recognized standard for the amount of insulation a lunch box or cooler provides. Shoppers should use their best judgment: Look at the thickness of the insulation, how rugged the fabric and seams are, and how well the insulated area closes.

How a construction worker lunch box is carried and how easily it opens and closes is also worth considering, so examine the soundness of handles and clasps. Those likely to pack ice in the lunch box should also check how leakproof it is, particularly with soft cool boxes.

All aspects of jobsite safety are important—even regarding your lunch box. Certain products previously used to produce plastics are now deemed unsafe for use with food. The organic compound bisphenol A (known as BPA) is one of the main culprits, though PVC and phthalates (which make plastics more flexible) should also be avoided. Many manufacturers will state whether their plastic containers are free of these materials. Since food hygiene is a crucial part of food safety, remember also to consider how easy it will be to thoroughly wash all areas of the container.

The guide above contains useful information and vetted products to help you choose the best lunch box for construction workers. Anyone with additional questions about how to choose and use a rugged, reliable lunch box will find more information below.

As with the best coolers, keeping lunch cold in a lunch box is best accomplished by using an insulated ice bag or box with ice blocks or bags of ice inside.

Hot soups and stews will maintain the desired temperature inside an insulated container or vacuum bottle. Plug-in warmers like the Travelisimo Electric Heated Lunch Box can also heat meals so long as a wall outlet or DC port is available.

The body can absorb aluminum through contact with food. However, many sources say it passes through naturally and does not present health problems. Some aluminum lunch boxes are specifically marked as food safe.

The best way to clean most lunch boxes is with a sponge and warm, soapy water, though the manufacturer may have its own suggestions, and these should take priority.

Health experts often suggest you replace your lunch box every year since even the best options can accumulate small amounts of mold and bacteria in hard-to-clean crevices. If damaged, a lunch box should be replaced immediately to prevent any risk of contamination.

Generally speaking, no, lunch boxes are not microwavable. If you need a microwavable container, consider packing something like these PrepNaturals glass meal-prep containers inside your lunch box.

Stainless steel lunch boxes aren’t necessarily better than plastic ones. However, they are a lightweight and durable option, especially for construction workers. This Stanley Classic 10-Quart Lunch Box is one of our absolute favorite steel lunch boxes.

#7831. What Happened to Cheap, Basic Cars?

"Feature creep" has left cars over-expensive and stuffed with technology. Is it even possible to go back to basics?

There was a time when buying a cheap new car was relatively simple. The answer might have involved crank windows, manual door locks, an AM/FM radio, and seats upholstered in something that looked suspiciously like industrial carpeting.

Today, the idea of a truly low-budget, no-frills vehicle is getting hard to find. Even the least expensive new cars come with touchscreens, driver-assistance systems, connectivity features, multiple airbags, and enough electronic wizardry to make a 1990s luxury car look like a farm tractor by comparison.

That raises a reasonable question: Can you still buy a genuinely inexpensive, basic vehicle in 2026? The short answer is yes, but “basic” no longer means what it used to.

Before we talk about what no-frills, low-budget vehicles are available, it’s important that we set a baseline for what that kind of car is in today’s market.

Modern safety and fuel economy technology are two of the biggest reasons today’s inexpensive vehicles don’t look anything like their ancestors. A new car sold in the United States must meet extensive federal safety requirements. That means airbags, stability control, rearview backup cameras, crash protection, and a long list of other requirements.

Consumers have also developed expectations. Try selling a new car without air conditioning today and see how quickly the internet catches fire. Nobody wants to return to the days when a buyer had to choose between air conditioning and an AM/FM radio. Budget buyers today expect power windows, remote locks, smartphone connectivity, and decent climate control.

The result is an interesting middle ground. Today’s cheapest cars aren’t truly bare-bones. Automakers have figured out how to put a surprising amount of technology into relatively inexpensive vehicles without necessarily making them luxury cars.

For years, the sub-$20,000 new car was the entry point for budget-conscious buyers. Models like the Mitsubishi Mirage, Nissan Versa, Chevrolet Spark, and various tiny hatchbacks gave shoppers an inexpensive way into a new vehicle.

Many of those cars are gone now. The market has steadily moved toward larger vehicles, more equipment, higher prices, and greater complexity. That doesn’t mean inexpensive cars have disappeared. It means the definition of inexpensive has moved upward. A buyer looking for a new vehicle in the low-$20,000 range can still find options, but those vehicles aren’t exactly stripped-down A-to-B appliances anymore.

Even inexpensive cars now tend to have infotainment screens, Bluetooth, backup cameras, automatic emergency braking, lane-departure warnings, and other features that were once the exclusive territory of expensive luxury models.

The economy in the U.S. has changed significantly. Not just from COVID and various political changes, but also from the general mindset of most Americans. When we compare pricing from 30 or even just 15 years ago, we often mentally skew the results due to our perspective of that change. It’s important to remember that, thanks to inflation, a dollar from 2011 is not a dollar in 2026. That ‘11 dollar is now $1.49. Inflation compounds and that 15 years has meant a 49 percent decrease in value for our money.

Knowing that, we can compare the average new vehicle purchase price (currently about $51,000) today with the average 15 years ago ($30,500). Then we can compare those values to the average household income from both eras: $50,000 in 2011 and $87,500 in 2026. Doing that, we find that things haven’t changed much.

The average new vehicle price seems very high compared to 15 years ago, but it was about 60 percent of the average household income in 2011 and is still that for 2026.

Yes and no. If your definition of low-budget means “I need reliable transportation and I don’t care whether it has the latest technology,” the used market is still where you’ll get a good deal. But a good deal doesn’t always mean good value. Shopping for a used vehicle is a whole discussion unto itself and countless books, videos, and articles have been made detailing the do’s and don’ts.

What’s important and relevant here is to realize that while a three- to seven-year-old compact car can provide much of the transportation value that new economy cars once offered, it will come with some downsides. The trick is to shop based on condition and ownership history rather than simply finding the cheapest four-door vehicle.

What’s more, the used car market has changed significantly since the COVID blip. Up until just before the shutdowns began, the used car market remained relatively steady in pricing versus the new car market, with long-term changes largely following inflation. During COVID, used car prices jumped by about 49 percent as demand for vehicles collided with a lack of new vehicles due to closures. Afterward, as new cars began to once again appear on dealership lots, the used car market eventually saw less demand and adjusted accordingly.

That adjustment, however, wasn’t back down to pre-COVID numbers. It’s still 17 percent higher than it was. And it seems to have decided to hold steady there. The reason used cars are much more expensive is, again, supply and demand. This time between used car availability and demand from buyers wanting them. There are fewer used cars being sold because owners are keeping their used cars longer. This disparity and its higher price result has been a big driver in new car sales for the past few years.

Yes, but you have to adjust your expectations. If your definition of “no-frills” is “nothing I don’t need,” the new-car market still has possibilities. If your definition is “give me an engine, four wheels, a steering wheel, and absolutely nothing else,” you’re probably shopping used or waiting on the upcoming Slate pickup truck.

#7830. Back At The Mayflower

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The first day of the 2026 Federalist Society Convention is in the can. There is much to report.

First, it is good to be back at the Mayflower--well at least good for those of us who made it in. Several years ago, FedSoc decided to move from the Mayflower to the Hilton, a much larger venue. The group had simply outgrown the classic hotel. The downside, of course, is that the Hilton is a terrible hotel. There were assassination attempts on two Presidents at the "Hinkley Hilton." There was no common meeting area, and attendees had to traverse a labyrinth of hallways between sessions. Worse, the rooms were a decade overdue for renovation. We hated it. But most of us were able to fit in.

This year, the registration for the national convention filled up almost instantaneously. I had planned to bring many of my students, but they simply never made it off the waiting list. Longtime members were hanging out in the lobby, hoping to make it off the waiting list, with no luck. I heard that the Harvard FedSoc chapter scheduled a conference for students who could not get in--apparently known as the "shadow docket." People complained to me, as if it was my fault we went back to the small Mayflower because of my carping about the Hilton. I get blamed for everything.

FedSoc will have to figure out what to do for next year, the 40th Anniversary of the National Lawyers Convention. We could always try to check out the new East Wing Ballroom, assuming Judge Leon doesn't enjoin it! The Gaylord Hotel in Maryland could fit everyone, but I am still scarred from the gala dinner there in 2016. I have long been a fan of holding the convention outside of D.C. It would send the exact right message. The times where people in D.C. offices can just stop by for a few panels are long gone. (The sold out registration means only those willing to attend the entire program will be there.) And anyone who wants to speak on the program of this platform should be willing to get on a flight. I would have recommended Texas for the venue, but we will soon be in hostile territory. Perhaps the free state of Florida is the last, best hope.

Second, the format of the FedSoc conference is different. I was so accustomed to the usual rhythm, I feel a bit disoriented. There are no breakout panels. Every panel is a "showcase" panel in the Grand Ballroom. The other rooms are overflow rooms with screens to watch the programming. The schedule is all different. The Rosenkranz Debate was on Thursday afternoon rather than Saturday afternoon over lunch. The Bork and Olson Lectures are both on Friday. And the program ends on Saturday at 2:15, about three hours earlier than usual. Also, instead of having lunchtime panels, all of the rooms on the second floor host smaller, intimate lunches. You could sit at a table with a judge and eight others to chat about an interesting topic. I was at Chief Judge Elrod's table to learn about the Lord of the Rings. (Trigger warning for commenters: I have never read any of those books, I fell asleep during the first movie, and never watched the others.) The discussion was fun! There are some judges who treat their judicial sinecures like Gollum treats the ring. How precious.

I see pros and cons to the new format. On the plus side, this format was far less overwhelming. I routinely felt drained by all of the content. Also, I always felt like I was missing something when I committed to a panel. As a result, I would often bounce between different panels, ensuring that I missed stuff. On the negative side, I enjoyed the ability to pick different panels that may be of interest. I thought the practice groups put on a wide arrange of topical panels. Moreover, there are far fewer speaking slots available with only a few panels each day. These are prime opportunities for up-and-coming members. Still, for this America 250 celebration, I liked the theme in which each panel was framed around a few words from the Declaration. This is an area I have studied for years, and I still learned quite a lot. I don't think we could have kept the Declaration theme going with breakouts.

Third, there is a much stronger focus on students--the lifeblood of Fedsoc. I appreciated that each panel was introduced by a student, rather than the chair of the practice group. During the Scalia dinner, the winners of the Feddie student chapter awards were asked to stand up. I am so proud of the South Texas Chapter, and my students Ryan Lanier and Makayla Arthur, for winning the Hamilton Award for "Most Improved Chapter." Matthew Weinberg, the President of the UCLA chapter during the Percival protest, was given a courage award. And each of the Soc! lunchtime tables was hosted by a student chapter leader.

We can never forget that FedSoc was founded by a bunch of law students. Old people (present company included) need to always give the youth these sorts of opportunities. It wasn't that long ago that I met Will Scharf at the Mayflower, and now he is White House Counsel. I can say the same for so many current judges and other officials that I met when I was student. Indeed, some of the current judges hosted me as a Professor at their chapters! (In 2033, I'll be 49.)  Everything that rises must converge.

Fourth, the decoration of the Mayflower and the Marriott Marquis ballroom was top-notch. There is red, white, and blue bunting all over the Grand Ballroom. The backdrop of the Scalia dinner was expertly done, topped off with George Washington's bible! (No, we couldn't touch it.) The Marine Corp band played during the processional. The Madison Club reception was no longer crammed into a tiny, dark, and noisy tent. It was held in a spacious atrium at the Marquis. Moreover, Madison Club members have access to Edgar's as a lounge to get food and snacks during the day. What a really, really smart idea. This sort of attention to detail matters, at least to me.

Fifth the security is intense. Registration is now available on the lower level. No one is allowed into the hallway without showing credentials and passing through a body scanner. Large bags are banned and smaller bags are searched. The busses from the Mayflower to the Marquis were swept for security, and there was a National Guardsman on board. It is a sad commentary that we have to take these precautions. But with an actual assassination attempt against Justice Kavanaugh, I think we have to accept these costs. (During the Scalia Dinner, Justice Alito praised the courage of Justices Kavanaugh and Barrett for joining the Dobbs decision, knowing what risks that could bring.)

Sixth, I was sort of expecting the vibe at the Mayflower to be grim in light of last week's election. I remember how the 2008 convention felt something like a funeral. I think the mood was mostly one of shock. There are efforts in play to figure out how to deal with the loss of Attorneys General in Texas, Ohio, Iowa, and Kansas. Other states will have to pick up the heavy lifting. Lawyers in Austin can find safe refuge in Baton Rouge, Jackson, St. Louis, Nashville, Tallahassee, Montgomery, and other cities. I am currently researching the laws of intervention on both the plaintiff and defendant side, confessions of error in criminal cases, as well as standing for state legislators and the state senate. The agenda has shifted.

Seventh, one thing I love about the National Convention is that business is conducted right in the hallways. There is a strong sentiment to do everything we can to confirm the remaining judges. These aren't quite the midnight judges of the outgoing Federalist Party, but we are in a similar mindset. There is a universal agreement that Judge Rudofsky was screwed. I second everything my friend Rob Luther wrote in this op-ed in the Arkansas newspaper. And there is a concerted effort to help Elliot Gaiser get across the finish line. What a complete waste if this seat is left for James Talarico to fill. Talk about cutting off your nose to spite your six-gendered face. And then there's Todd Butler. Had the election turned out differently, things may have gone differently. But he is on the path to confirmation. I hope Butler proves me wrong--and he will have a quick opportunity to do so. The January en banc siting has a huge 922(g) case and a challenge to Texas's social media law. As for the new Eighth Circuit nominee, Cody Hiland, he have to prove a lot of people wrong.

#7829. 3 Winterization Projects That Are as Easy as Painting

100+ Most Unique and Practical Gifts 🎁 for Homeowners and DIYers

Published Nov 11, 2026 10:30 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Tips, tricks & ideas for a better home and yard, delivered to your inbox daily.

Winter weather can be devastating to outdoor furniture, appliances, and structures, which is why many people store as much as possible in a covered shed or garage throughout the cold season. Even though not everything can be neatly tucked away, such as your deck, walkways, and gates, you can take steps to prepare them for harsh winter conditions before snow starts to fall.

Outdoor winterization projects that involve painting, staining, or sealing help surfaces create a durable barrier against freeze-thaw cycles, moisture intrusion, and corrosive deicing salts. It’s important to complete these protective jobs before the first hard freeze so you can prevent deep structural damage during the winter months.

Leaving wood decks, fences, or patio furniture bare during winter allows moisture from snow and ice to seep into the wood pores. When trapped water freezes, it expands, causing the wood to split, warp, and rot. A fresh coat of waterproof sealant or oil-based stain acts as a hydrophobic barrier. Water pools on top of the sealed surface rather than penetrating the wood grain.

Before applying a compatible exterior stain or water-repellent finish, clean the surface, remove failing finish, and allow the wood to dry sufficiently. For decking and steps, choose a winterization product specifically approved for horizontal surfaces and foot traffic.

Marc Sharkey, owner of Dynamic Painting Inc, says that “the finish reduces water absorption from rain and melting snow. Repeated wetting and drying can contribute to checking, splitting, and warping; prolonged dampness also creates conditions for decay.

“Pay particular attention to exposed board ends and areas where the old finish has worn away.” He also warns: “A new coating cannot repair rotten wood.” Given that Sharkey’s business is based in Alberta, he has experience dealing with some of the harshest winters in North America.

This oil-based formula provides corrosion resistance and weather protection for outdoor metal surfaces . Learn more in our buyer’s guide.

Winter preparation is important to safeguard your home. Chipped paint on steel or iron railings, furniture, and gates exposes the raw metal to oxygen and winter humidity, rapidly accelerating the oxidation process. Road salt or salt-based sidewalk ice melts further expedite this corrosion, eating through the metal structures. Applying a coat of exterior, rust-resistant enamel or oil-based paint seals out moisture and oxygen, halting the chemical reaction that creates rust.

It’s a budget-friendly winterization project that also forms a slick, chemical-resistant barrier against salt splash-back. Before applying a coating, remove loose rust and flaking paint and clean away dirt and salt. Then apply an appropriate rust-inhibiting primer and exterior metal finish. Check compatibility carefully: steel, aluminum, and galvanized metal can require different preparation and primers.

“An intact coating limits exposure to moisture and oxygen, helping slow corrosion. Left exposed, rust can spread beneath surrounding paint, causing more peeling and pitting. Over time, severe corrosion can weaken components. Painting over loose rust does not solve the underlying problem,” explains Sharkey.

Moisture from ice and snow can cause significant damage to concrete because it is a highly porous material. When snow melts on walkways, driveways, or patios, the concrete absorbs the water. Subsequent freezing temperatures cause that internal water to expand, which leads to surface flaking, scaling, and deep cracking.

Unlike surface coatings, penetrating sealers chemically bond inside concrete pores. They create an invisible, breathable hydrophobic barrier that prevents liquid water from sinking into the stone, while still allowing internal vapor to escape.

Sharkey notes that “for compatible, absorbent concrete steps, walkways, or patios, a penetrating sealer rated for exterior concrete and freeze-thaw exposure can reduce water absorption. Confirm compatibility with any existing treatment and follow the preparation instructions.”

Reducing water and deicing-salt penetration helps protect against winter deterioration. However, just keep in mind that a sealer is preventive maintenance; it does not repair cracks, failing concrete, or drainage problems.

#7827. What’s Downshifting? The Trend That’s Helping Homeowners Do More With Less

Downshifting can mean a smaller home, fewer belongings, or a lighter schedule. Here's how the lifestyle works and where to start.

Sometimes less IS more. At least, that’s what one home and lifestyle trend would have you believe.

A house can demand more time and money than homeowners expect. Spare bedrooms fill up with things nobody uses, the yard needs another afternoon of work, and there’s always something that needs fixing. Downshifting is one way homeowners are trying to change that.

Here’s what downshifting means, how it’s different from downsizing, and whether it can actually save money.

A post shared by RetroSuburbia (@retrosuburbiaofficial)

Downshifting is pretty much what it sounds like. It’s a decision to slow things down a bit, spend less, and get rid of some of the things that take up too much time or space around the house.

Permaculture writer David Holmgren covers the idea in his book RetroSuburbia, which describes downshifting as “a conscious choice and action to shift to a lifestyle with less consumption, complexity, stress and status seeking.” The idea is to make everyday life a little easier to manage, whether that’s by cutting expenses or having fewer responsibilities.

It sounds a lot like downsizing, but the two aren’t quite the same. Downsizing usually means moving to a smaller house or getting rid of belongings. Downshifting doesn’t necessarily involve moving at all.

One family might trade a large house for a smaller place that needs less maintenance. Another might stay right where they are, stop buying things they don’t need, or spend less time working on the house.

Homeowners can start by looking at what’s taking up the most time or money. Maybe that’s a garage full of things that haven’t been used in years, or a spare bedroom that’s become a storage room. Clearing out those spaces can mean less to clean and look after.

Other changes can be pretty small, too. Borrowing a tool instead of buying one, fixing furniture rather than replacing it, or starting a small vegetable garden are all examples. The Environmental Protection Agency also recommends buying less and reusing things to help reduce waste.

Even looking for ways to lower utility bills, like sealing drafty windows or keeping up with heating and cooling maintenance, can be part of downshifting.

One reason people consider downshifting is to save money. Buying fewer things and using less energy can certainly help, but moving to a smaller home doesn’t automatically mean smaller bills.

“New homeowners are often surprised by the costs of owning property,” according to the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau. The agency recommends putting together a budget that includes property taxes, insurance, repairs, and other expenses beyond the mortgage.

There are some practical things to consider, too. A smaller house might not have enough room for a growing family, and moving farther away could mean a longer commute. Even growing vegetables or repairing things around the house takes time.

Still, for some households, having fewer things to pay for and maintain can leave more time for family, hobbies, or just enjoying the house they already have.

And that’s really the point of downshifting. It doesn’t have to mean selling a house or getting rid of everything. Sometimes it’s as simple as deciding the house doesn’t need another project or another piece of furniture.

#7826. At Large Circuit Nominees?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

If the blue slip is abolished for district courts, it should be obliterated for circuit courts.

During the first Trump Administration, the blue slip policy was effectively eliminated for circuit court judges. The goal, of course, was to ensure that states with one or more Democratic senators would not be able to block all circuit court nominees. Still, the blue slip policy remained for district court judges through Trump 1.0, the Biden Administration, and Trump 2.0. Does anyone expect the blue slip policy for district court judges to survive if a Democrat wins the White House in 2028 with 56+ Senators? I am doubtful. Indeed, given how Democrats blocked so many U.S. Attorney nominees, I am doubtful the blue slip endures even for that position.

Let's just assume the blue slip policy is eliminated for district court judges. Should the Republicans ever regain power, I propose a thought experiment: actually eliminate the blue slip for circuit judges. As I've noted, circuit court judges belong to the circuit, not the state. It is a mistake to even think of a "home state senator" for a circuit court seat. Of course seats are affiliated with a state by virtue of custom, but nothing in the statute requires it. If Congress wants to assign a seat to a state, they can easily do so. But a Circuit Court Judge decides cases that affect all of the states in a circuit. Indeed, over time, some seats have "switched" between states.

The President could perhaps facilitate that process by making all circuit court nominees "at large." In other words, the President could solicit nominees from candidates in all states in that circuit. If a Fifth Circuit seat opens up, the Senators from Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi could all make recommendations, and the President could pick the best candidate all around. Likewise, if an Eighth Circuit seat opens up, the Senators from the states between North Dakota and Arkansas can make recommendations.

First, and foremost, requiring this much consultation can gum up the process. Dealing with one set of senators is a lot of work. Multiplying that by many more can become impossible. But it would be just that--a consultation. The White House would only have to interview the judges that clear the bar. Again, no actual blue slip. I suspect if you rank all of the nominees circuit-wide, few would make the cut.

Second, some senators are very good at picking judges. Opening up the process to so many not-so-good senators, can make the process worse. Indeed, Senators are democratically accountable, while people in OLP and the White House Counsel's Office are largely unknown. I think the response is that very few few Senators are actually good at this process. My goodness, the Senators from Mississippi and Arkansas should be permanently disqualified from picking their friends as judges. I think my recommendation would, on balance, get far more strong judges than the status quo. Of course, the President can give more deference to senators with proven track records of picking judges.

Third, Senators are unlikely to go along with this process, and will not give up their customary prerogative. Again, in my hypothetical, the blue slip is gone for district court judges, so it will be a different world. Indeed, given that district court judges can issue universal vacaturs that affect the entire country, I'm not sure why senators should have that much control. The Senate can of course vote down a nominee, but that would have to be a vote they are accountable for. Would Senators Boozman and Cotton have voted down Judge Rudofsky on the floor? Probably not.

This is just a thought experiment. Fodder to consider for the future. That is, unless the Grand Old Party goes the way of the Federalists and the Whigs.

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

After researching and comparing product features and reviews for dozens of nonstick snow blower sprays, we narrowed our testing list to eight products. We applied each snow blower nonstick spray in a dry location, fully covering the chutes, augers, interior boxes, and passageways. A large portion of our work coincided with our tests on snow blowers for gravel driveways, meaning the sprays were all used in particularly rough conditions since the snow contained dirt and hard particles. We also tested them on shovels, plow blades, door locks, and other surfaces needing lubrication to get a comprehensive idea of how long each spray remained effective, their ease of application, and their overall performance.

Before choosing a nonstick spray, take a few minutes to learn what to look for, including drying time, safety concerns, functions, and the spray’s longevity.

The drying time for a spray wax for snow blowers will vary depending on the specific product, the temperature and humidity of the environment, and the moisture content in the snow blower’s chute. Products that dry quickly are generally easier to use since they make applying a second layer when needed faster so you can get to work sooner.

Applying the nonstick snow and ice repellent in a warm, dry environment, like a garage or workshop, is ideal. Warmth helps the spray stick to the metal and dry quickly. Users can apply sprays to damp surfaces in freezing temperatures, but it will take longer for the spray to dry. Until the spray is completely dry, it won’t lubricate properly, nor will it be fully water- or corrosion-resistant.

While nonstick sprays for snow blowers are helpful in preventing clogs, they often contain chemicals that warrant handling them with care. We recommend you check the product’s label for safe application recommendations and to see if it contains any hazardous materials.

Generally speaking, you’ll want to keep snow blower sprays out of reach of children and pets since they can be toxic if ingested or inhaled. It’s a good idea to use these products in a well-ventilated space and consider wearing eye protection, a respirator, and gloves. Because the liquid spray may be flammable until it dries, store it away from sources of heat or flames.

The primary purpose of a nonstick spray for snow blowers is to lubricate the inside of the snow blower chute to keep snow from sticking and clogging the chute. However, many nonstick sprays have additional benefits, such as preventing rust, protecting against ultraviolet (UV) damage, resisting water, or even adding a shine to metal finishes.

Longevity refers to the length of time a nonstick spray remains effective after application. Every nonstick spray we tested must be reapplied frequently, though some worked well through several uses. Generally speaking, they all need to be reapplied every few uses at a minimum.

When working through a really difficult storm, consider reapplying nonstick spray after every use to keep the machine performing optimally. Always apply a fresh coat ahead of storms and continue renewing the coating as needed throughout the season. Even if you go through a couple of cans in the winter, you will still save money removing snow yourself rather than paying the cost of professional snow removal.

Snow blower chutes can clog because you’re trying to push through the snow too fast. They also clog when the heavy snow has a high moisture content and forms compact clumps that stick to the sides of the chute.

You can use normal WD-40 to help lubricate the auger and moving parts on a snow blower. Use the silicone version of the product to add a nonstick layer of protection on the snow blower chute and auger. It’s easy to apply, dries quickly, and acts as a water repellent and corrosion inhibitor.

Snow blower spray is easy to use: Just shake the can, remove the lid, and spray an even coating inside the chute and to the auger. The nonstick spray lubricant makes the chute and auger slippery, preventing snow from sticking and clogging the blower.
